name: Thomas theorem
statement: If people define situations as real, they are real in their consequences: what a situation means to the people in it governs what they do, and what they do has effects.
meaning: Action follows the meaning a situation carries for the person in it, and the consequences of that action are real whatever the situation was in objective terms. The sentence is the last line of a methodological argument rather than a general law. Its chapter defends the case history, the life record and the psychoanalytic confession against the objection, which the Thomases attribute to the school of behaviourism, that introspective records have no validity. Their answer is that a subject's account reveals the situation that conditioned the behaviour, and that this holds even for a record as far from objective reality as a delusion of persecution. Merton kept the theorem separate from the self-fulfilling prophecy, and the difference is one clause. The prophecy needs the opening definition to be false. The theorem does not.

origin.who: W. I. Thomas and Dorothy Swaine Thomas
origin.where: The Child in America: Behavior Problems and Programs (New York: Alfred A. Knopf), page 572
origin.note: The sentence closes a paragraph on the evidential value of subjective records. Its illustration is an inmate of Dannemora prison who had killed several people who talked to themselves in the street, because he read insults off the movement of their lips and behaved as if that were true. The eponym is Merton's. He wrote of 'W. I. Thomas's sociological theorem' in 1938 and used 'the Thomas theorem' in his 1948 paper on the self-fulfilling prophecy.

evidence: There is no study behind the theorem. It is one sentence, supported by one anecdote which the Thomases report at second hand from a prison warden, in a chapter about research method. Merton's 1948 use added no data either: his illustration is a fictional bank called the Last National, and his stated point is that the same thought had been set out before Thomas by Bossuet, Mandeville, Marx, Freud and Sumner. In 1995 he added Epictetus and Schopenhauer, and noted that George Herbert Mead had told his Chicago classes that 'If a thing is not recognized as true, then it does not function as true in the community', a formulation published in 1936 which then sank. What has been measured is the sentence's circulation. Merton reports that none of the reviews of The Child in America in the American Journal of Sociology, Social Forces or Sociology and Social Research took any notice of the theorem. Kimball Young made it a chapter epigraph in his Social Psychology in 1930 and in Social Attitudes in 1931, both times without a source reference, and those epigraphs became the route by which it spread. R. S. Smith surveyed well over 100 introductory sociology textbooks and found 40 that quoted or paraphrased the theorem, of which one cited the book and page it came from. By Merton's count W. I. Thomas put the sentence in print three times in his career: the 1928 book, an essay in a 1931 Brookings Institution symposium, and Blumer's 1939 appraisal of The Polish Peasant. He never developed it.

replication.headline: No replication or direct empirical test of the theorem was located. The nearest experimental evidence belongs to the self-fulfilling prophecy, which is a narrower claim and has its own entry.
replication.detail: The theorem is not an experimental prediction. It names no population, no manipulation and no outcome, and Merton calls the sentence in its original setting an 'essentially methodological observation'. There is nothing in it that a repetition could confirm or overturn in the way an effect size can. The literature that does run experiments is the expectancy work, which sits in this atlas under self-fulfilling prophecy at entry 44 and the Pygmalion effect at entry 9. Those studies test something stronger and more specific: that a false expectation held by one person changes the behaviour of another, measurably, without either party knowing. Results there are mixed, and they are not evidence for or against the Thomases' sentence. A reader who wants numbers should go to those entries and should not treat a finding about teacher expectations as a test of the theorem.

limits: Searches for a replication or a direct empirical test covered Crossref's bibliographic index and web searches pairing the theorem with 'replication', 'empirical test', 'experiment' and 'hypothesis'. They returned commentary, applications and citation studies, and nothing that put the proposition at risk. The only counting exercise located is Smith's textbook survey, which measures how the sentence is cited rather than whether it holds. Smith's papers of 1995 and 1999 were not opened, because the publisher refused access; his argument and his 1993 figures are quoted here as Merton reproduces them, which is one remove from Smith. Merton's 1938 paper was not opened, so the page carrying his first use of the eponym is taken from his 1995 account, which gives it as 333 in the running text and as 331 to 332 in a letter reprinted in the same article. That 1995 article was read as a scan in Eugene Garfield's Merton collection at the University of Pennsylvania, with optical character recognition errors throughout. Dorothy Swaine Thomas's 1973 letter survives only as Merton reproduced it in that article, and no reply from her to his later published claims about it was located.
misreadings: The theorem is routinely credited to W. I. Thomas alone. Merton did that first and defended it for the rest of his life, on the strength of a letter Dorothy Swaine Thomas wrote him on 10 September 1973, saying that Thomas had employed her as an assistant after the Rockefeller group told him to get himself a statistician, that 'The statistical portions were mine' and that 'The concept of "defining the situation" was strictly W.I.'s.' Smith's answer is that the sentence appears in a jointly authored book, in a chapter with no separate attribution, so both names belong on it unless there is compelling evidence otherwise. The disagreement is about what a private letter settles, not about who signed the book. Smith also found that most textbooks name W. I. Thomas alone and that the few citing the book often drop its second author. The wording drifts as well. Willard Waller quoted it in 1938 as 'If people define things as real, they are real in their consequences', altering two words. Howard P. Becker located it on page 79 of the one-volume Polish Peasant, where Merton reports it is not to be found, and concluded that it was 'probably Znaniecki's'. The theorem is also not the self-fulfilling prophecy, which requires the first definition to be wrong. Merton's own warning is against the strong reading, in which only definitions are held to determine anything, and which converts the theorem into the maxim that if men do not define situations as real, they are not real.

sources.text: Thomas, W. I., & Thomas, D. S. (1928). The Child in America: Behavior Problems and Programs. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. The theorem and its Dannemora illustration read on page 572 of a scan of the first edition.
